items.item: Compatibility mode isn't a property of an evolution alone — the same change (removing a field) passes under one mode and would fail under a stricter one, which is why choosing the mode is itself a design decision, not a formality.

at.step: Reveal: the same evolution, two different gates

items.item: Backward being the default isn't arbitrary — it's specifically what lets consumers rewind to the beginning of a topic and still read every historical record, a guarantee forward compatibility doesn't give.

at.step: Reveal: backward, forward, full, transitive

items.item: Avro and Protobuf don't just enforce compatibility differently — they disagree on the more basic question of what makes two fields 'the same field' across versions (name vs. position), which is why a safe rename in one format is unsafe in the other.

at.step: Reveal: three formats, three native behaviors

items.item: JSON Schema having no native evolution model isn't a minor gap — it means every compatibility guarantee for JSON Schema in this registry is entirely a product of the registry's own layered rules, not anything the format itself enforces.

at.step: Reveal: three formats, three native behaviors

items.item: A subject-naming strategy is really a decision about blast radius: TopicNameStrategy makes every record type on a topic share one compatibility fate, while RecordNameStrategy isolates each type's own evolution from the others.

items.item: Carrying only a schema id in the wire format, not the schema itself, is what makes compatibility checking a registry-side concern rather than a per-message cost — every message stays small regardless of how large the schema actually is.

items.item: A technically compatible evolution passing every mode this topic teaches can still be semantically wrong, which is exactly the gap a data contract is built to close — compatibility and correctness are related but not the same question.
